1  the prior ruling nor new facts or legal authority that could not have been raised 
2  earlier.  See ECF No. 58 at 11.  The Court denies the Motion.             

3                         LEGAL STANDARD                                     
4       “As long as a district court has jurisdiction over the case, then it possesses 
5  the inherent procedural power to reconsider, rescind, or modify an interlocutory 

6  order for cause seen by it to be sufficient.”  City of Los Angeles, Harbor Div. v. 
7  Santa Monica Baykeeper, 254 F.3d 882, 885 (9th Cir. 2001) (quoting Melancon v. 
8  Texaco, Inc., 659 F.2d 551, 553 (5th Cir. 1981)) (quotation marks and emphasis 
9  omitted).  However, “[m]otions for reconsideration are disfavored and are not the 

10  place for parties to make new arguments not raised in their original briefs and 
11  arguments.”  Ramirez v. Medtronic, Inc., 961 F. Supp. 2d 977, 1005 (D. Ariz. 
12  2013) (citing Nw. Acceptance Corp. v. Lynnwood Equip., Inc., 841 F.2d 918, 925-

13  26 (9th Cir. 1988)); see also Cooper v. Tokyo Elec. Power Co., Inc., 166 F. Supp. 
14  3d 1103, 1116 (S.D. Cal. 2015) (citing Kona Enters., Inc. v. Est. of Bishop, 229 
15  F.3d 877, 890 (9th Cir. 2000)); Cachil Dehe Band of Wintun Indians of Colusa 
16  Indian Comm’ty v. California, 649 F. Supp. 2d 1063, 1069 (E.D. Cal. 2009) (citing 

17  Carroll v. Nakatani, 342 F.3d 934, 945 (9th Cir. 2003) and 389 Orange St. 
18  Partners v. Arnold, 179 F.3d 656, 665 (9th Cir. 1999)).                   
19       As set forth in in the Bench Trial Scheduling Order, the Court requires that a 

20  motion to reconsider show manifest error in the prior ruling or reveal new facts or 
1  legal authority which could not have been brought to the Court’s attention earlier.  
2  ECF No. 58 at 11.                                                         

3                            DISCUSSION                                      
4       Plaintiffs’ Motion, which they filed less than two months before the previous 
5  bench trial date in this case, asks the Court to vacate its summary judgment order 

6  and reopen discovery on the issue of damages.  The Motion is premised on an 
7  inaccurate recitation of the history of this case, particularly the events of the 
8  October 2024 discovery disputes, Plaintiffs’ belated Motion to Amend, and the 
9  reasons why the Court granted Defendant’s Motion for Summary Judgment.  When 

10  viewed against the record, Plaintiffs’ arguments for reconsideration lack merit.   
11    A. Discovery Orders                                                     
12       Pursuant to the initial Bench Trial Scheduling Order dated May 1, 2024, the 

13  parties had until January 10, 2025, to complete discovery.  ECF No. 25 at 16.   
14       Discovery disputes arose in September 2024.  See ECF Nos. 30, 39.  In the 
15  dispute relevant here, Plaintiffs moved to compel Defendant to respond to 
16  Plaintiffs’ Request for Production No. 3 (“RFP 3”).  ECF No. 30 at 5-6.  By that 

17  time, Plaintiffs had narrowed RFP 3 to require production of “any and all 
18  documents that refer or relate to sales of Bac-Stop, whether or not it was sold by or 
19  for [the alleged partnership between Plaintiffs and Defendant], including, without 

20  limitation, invoices, bill of sales [sic], bill of ladings [sic], purchase orders and/or 
1  any other document evidence the sale [sic] of Bac Stop,” ECF No. 32-1 at 3-4 
2  (underlining in original), for sales made in “the period of March 15, 2020[,] 

3  through September 17, 2020,” ECF No. 32-3 at 1 (underlining in original), in 
4  “Washington, Oregon, California, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, and Montana,” ECF 
5  No. 32-4 at 1-2.  This request was based on Plaintiffs’ contention that they 

6  acquired new customers from these states who bought Defendant’s Bac Stop  
7  product in this timeframe, and that the records from these sales may have omitted 
8  reference to Plaintiffs due to administrative oversight.  ECF No. 30 at 3-4; see also 
9  ECF No. 43 at 2-4.  The timeframe and geographic limitations were key to  

10  defining the appropriate scope of RFP No. 3, as Plaintiffs were apparently unable 
11  to identify the relevant customers.  See ECF Nos. 32-4, 32-5.             
12       Defendant contended that RFP 3 was still overbroad and unduly        

13  burdensome, ECF No. 41, but at the October 15, 2024, discovery hearing, defense 
14  counsel could not explain what type and magnitude of burden Defendant would 
15  face in responding to RFP 3.  The Court directed Defendant to respond to RFP 3 
16  under the time-period and geographic limitations to which Plaintiffs had already 

17  agreed.  ECF No. 52 at 3.  Given the delay caused by the discovery dispute, the 
18  Court directed the parties to propose an amended scheduling order based on their 
19  determination of a feasible pretrial schedule.  Id. at 2.                 

20                                                                            
1       On October 30, 2024, the Court held a further discovery dispute hearing.  
2  ECF No. 55.  Shortly before the hearing, Defendant filed the declaration of one of 

3  its employees, Theodore Thome.  ECF No. 54.  Mr. Thome attested that a full 
4  response to RFP 3 would require Defendant’s employees to assemble “over 1,500 
5  document packets” spanning 91 customers by manually reviewing each customer’s 

6  file for responsive documents.  Id. at 2 ¶¶ 4-6.  He estimated this task would take 
7  two employees, working four hours per day, up to four weeks.  Id. at ¶ 6.  He 
8  attached a list of the 91 customers identified, organized according to the date 
9  Defendant established them as customers.  ECF No. 54-1.  Most had establishment 

10  dates well before any of the events alleged in the Second Amended Complaint, let 
11  alone before the alleged partnership.1                                    
12       At the hearing, Defendant noted that the Second Amended Complaint    

13  alleged that the partnership between Plaintiffs and Defendant began in “summer of 
14  2020” and argued that RFP 3 could logically be narrowed to Bac Stop sales 
15  involving the four or five customers who had not already been established 
16                                                                            

17                                                                            
18                                                                            

19  1 33 customers were established in 2020, and 4 customers were established in 
20  2019.  The remaining 54 were established between 2002 and 2018.           
1  customers of Defendant before summer 2020.2  Plaintiffs’ counsel argued that the 
2  alleged partnership began in summer 2019 and that she was “blindsided” by the 

3  contention that it began in summer 2020.  The Court observed that Defendant was 
4  relying on the Second Amended Complaint, wherein Plaintiffs alleged that they 
5  and Defendant agreed to enter into a partnership agreement “during the summer of 

6  2020.”3  ECF No. 17 at 5-6 ¶ 17.  Plaintiffs’ counsel contended she had evidence 
7  that would prove the partnership began earlier and began showing various unfiled 
8  documents in open court, though these documents raised more questions than they 
9  answered.  See ECF No. 70 at 6.                                           

10       The Court concluded that the scope of discovery was governed by the  
11  allegations in the operative pleadings, therefore only Bac Stop sales to customers 
12  who became established with Defendant in summer 2020 would be relevant.  But 

13  out of caution, the Court defined “summer 2020” more broadly, to include  
14                                                                            

15  2 Defendant apparently interpreted the “summer of 2020” timeframe Plaintiffs 
16  alleged to have begun around June 1, 2020.  See ECF No. 54-1 at 2 (reflecting four 
17  customers with establishment dates in June or July 2020).                 
18  3 The original Complaint and the Amended Complaint included the same allegation 
19  that the partnership began in “the summer of 2020.”  ECF No. 70 at 3 (quoting 

20  ECF No. 1-1 at 8 ¶ 3.10; ECF No. 4 at 5-6 ¶ 17).                          
1  May 2020.  ECF No. 56.  Accordingly, Defendant was required to produce Bac 
2  Stop sales records for a total of sixteen customers: the four included in Defendant’s 

3  proposed definition of summer 2020, plus twelve established in May 2020.  See 
4  ECF No. 54-1 at 2.                                                        
5       On November 14, 2024, the Court issued the Second Bench Trial Scheduling 

6  Order in accordance with the parties’ proposed schedule.  ECF No. 58 at 16; see 
7  also ECF No. 57 at 2.  The parties did not seek any further rulings on discovery 
8  disputes in the remaining discovery period.  On one occasion, the Court set a 
9  further discovery dispute hearing at Plaintiffs’ request, ECF No. 71, but the day 

10  before the related briefing deadline, the parties requested that the hearing be struck, 
11  ECF No. 72.                                                               
12       Plaintiffs’ Motion misrepresents these events, claiming that the Court 

13  narrowed RFP 3 “by reducing the 1,500 packets for customers to 4 packets for 
14  customers,” despite that Mr. Thome “admitted” these 1,500 packets “are relevant 
15  to Plaintiffs[’] claim for Bac Stop damages.”  ECF No. 109 at 5, 9.  The Court’s 
16  second Order directed Defendant to disclose records for the sixteen customers who 

17  were established in May 2020 or later for sales in Plaintiffs’ specified timeframe 
18  and geographic region.  It is unclear how many document packets existed for these 
19  sixteen customers.  But it is untrue that the Court limited the scope of RFP 3 to 

20  “4 packets,” or even to the packets for the four customers Defendant suggested.   
1       Plaintiffs missed all appropriate opportunities to reraise this issue if they had 
2  valid reason for the Court to reconsider the Order.  They did not seek any further 

3  ruling from the Court on this issue.  While they argue Mr. Thome gave     
4  contradicting testimony about the above facts at his deposition on April 23, 2025, 
5  ECF No. 109 at 5-6, they did not cite this section of his testimony as a basis for a 

6  further discovery dispute hearing, nor did they mention it in opposing Defendant’s 
7  Motion for Summary Judgment.4  Until now, Plaintiffs had never contended they 
8  were entitled to all of the approximately 1,500 document packets Mr. Thome 
9  described.  A party cannot use a motion for reconsideration to make new   

10  arguments not raised in their original briefs.  See Ramirez, 961 F. Supp. 2d at 1005.   
11                                                                            
12                                                                            

   4 Plaintiffs only mentioned Mr. Thome briefly in their opposition to summary

2  Plaintiffs provide no explanation of how records of Defendant’s sales to customers 

3  it had acquired long before the alleged partnership began could be relevant to their 
4  claims.  The Court has also reviewed the sections of Mr. Thome’s testimony that 
5  Plaintiffs cite and disagrees that his testimony contradicts his earlier  

6  representations in relation to RFP 3.                                     
7       Plaintiffs have not shown manifest error in the prior ruling, or new facts or 
8  legal authority which could not have been brought to the Court’s attention earlier, 
9  that warrants reconsideration of the Order limiting RFP 3 to the sixteen customers 

10  who were established with Defendant in May 2020 or later.                 
11    B. Plaintiffs’ Motion to Amend                                          
12       Although Plaintiffs do not request reconsideration of the Order denying 

13  leave to amend, the Court notes that Plaintiffs omit any mention why the Court 
14  denied them leave to amend, while portraying their efforts as “diligent.”  See ECF 
15  No. 109 at 5 n.3 (“Plaintiffs then moved for leave to amend the SAC to correct the 
16  erroneous dates . . ., which this Court denied . . .”) (citing ECF Nos. 60, 70), 8 

17  (“Defendant has refused to produce such evidence, despite diligent efforts by 
18  Plaintiffs to request, compel and even amend pleadings to obtain.”) (emphasis 
19  added).  The primary reason the Court denied Plaintiffs leave to amend was 

20  because they failed to provide any arguments or evidence of their own diligence, 
1  while the rest of the record strongly indicated they had not acted diligently.  See 
2  ECF No. 70 at 10-12.                                                      

3    C. Summary Judgment                                                     
4       Finally, Defendant moved for partial summary judgment on the contention 
5  that Plaintiffs had no evidence of the existence of unallocated Bac Stop damages to 

6  which they were entitled, except for a bare assertion by Michael Harvey,  
7  Defendant’s former CEO, that such damages existed and approximated        
8  $411,768.38.  ECF No. 79 at 14.  The Court concluded that Plaintiffs had not 
9  established that Mr. Harvey had personal knowledge about facts related to 

10  unattributed Bac Stop sales, was competent to testify on that subject, or had any 
11  basis besides speculation for his attestation of the amount of those damages.  ECF 
12  No. 96 at 15.  Plaintiffs offered nothing else except for their experts’ reports on 

13  unallocated Bac Stop damages, in which their experts explicitly stated that their 
14  opinions on unallocated Bac Stop damages depended entirely on Mr. Harvey’s 
15  declaration.  ECF No. 96 at 13-14; accord ECF No. 109 at 11-12.           
16       This was not, as Plaintiffs argue, a weighing of Mr. Harvey’s credibility or 

17  of the substantive elements of Plaintiffs’ claim.  See ECF No. 109 at 10, 12.  Both 
18  federal and Washington courts require competent evidence to support a claim for 
19  damages, as Plaintiffs acknowledge.  See ECF No. 109 at 11 (quoting Fed. Signal 

20  Corp. v. Safety Factors, Inc., 886 P.2d 172, 188 (Wash. 1994)).  If they relied on a 
1  witness’s declaration, they had to establish that the witness was competent to 
2  testify on those issues and was testifying from personal knowledge.  ECF No. 96 at 

3  4 (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(4)).5  They failed to do so, and they did not 
4  attempt to provide any other competent evidence of unallocated Bac Stop   
5  damages.6                                                                 

6                                                                            
7                                                                            

8  5 Plaintiffs suggest that the federal rules and Washington rules differ on this point, 
9  which is incorrect.  Compare Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(4) (“An affidavit or declaration 
10  used to support or oppose a motion must be made on personal knowledge, set out 
11  facts that would be admissible in evidence, and show that the affiant or declarant is 
12  competent to testify on the matters stated.”), with Wash. Super. Ct. Civ. R. 56(e) 

13  (“Supporting and opposing affidavits shall be made on personal knowledge, shall 
14  set forth such facts as would be admissible in evidence, and shall show   
15  affirmatively that the affiant is competent to testify to the matters stated therein.”).   
16  6 Apparently there was no “shred of evidence” of unallocated Bac Stop sales in the 

17  sales records for the sixteen customers established in “summer of 2020” that 
18  Plaintiffs were permitted to obtain under the second discovery order, as Plaintiffs 
19  offered none of those records in opposing summary judgment.  See ECF No. 109 at 

20  2 (alleging that the second discovery order is the reason “why Plaintiffs are not in 
1       Plaintiffs have not shown manifest error in the prior ruling, or new facts or 
2  legal authority which could not have been brought to the Court’s attention earlier, 

3  that warrants reconsideration of the Order granting Defendant summary judgment 
4  on the claim for unallocated Bac Stop damages.                            
5       Accordingly, IT IS HEREBY ORDERED:                                   

6       1.   Plaintiffs’ Motion for Reconsideration, ECF No. 109, is DENIED.   
7       IT IS SO ORDERED.  The District Court Executive is directed to enter this 
8  Order and provide copies to the parties.                                  
9            DATED November 20, 2025.                                        

10                            s/Mary K. Dimke

3    C. Summary Judgment                                                     
4       Finally, Defendant moved for partial summary judgment on the contention 
5  that Plaintiffs had no evidence of the existence of unallocated Bac Stop damages to 

6  which they were entitled, except for a bare assertion by Michael Harvey,  
7  Defendant’s former CEO, that such damages existed and approximated        
8  $411,768.38.  ECF No. 79 at 14.  The Court concluded that Plaintiffs had not 
9  established that Mr. Harvey had personal knowledge about facts related to 

10  unattributed Bac Stop sales, was competent to testify on that subject, or had any 
11  basis besides speculation for his attestation of the amount of those damages.  ECF 
12  No. 96 at 15.  Plaintiffs offered nothing else except for their experts’ reports on 

13  unallocated Bac Stop damages, in which their experts explicitly stated that their 
14  opinions on unallocated Bac Stop damages depended entirely on Mr. Harvey’s 
15  declaration.  ECF No. 96 at 13-14; accord ECF No. 109 at 11-12.           
16       This was not, as Plaintiffs argue, a weighing of Mr. Harvey’s credibility or 

17  of the substantive elements of Plaintiffs’ claim.  See ECF No. 109 at 10, 12.  Both 
18  federal and Washington courts require competent evidence to support a claim for 
19  damages, as Plaintiffs acknowledge.  See ECF No. 109 at 11 (quoting Fed. Signal 

20  Corp. v. Safety Factors, Inc.,
886 P.2d 172, 188
 (Wash. 1994)).  If they relied on a 
1  witness’s declaration, they had to establish that the witness was competent to 
2  testify on those issues and was testifying from personal knowledge.  ECF No. 96 at 

3  4 (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(4)).5  They failed to do so, and they did not 
4  attempt to provide any other competent evidence of unallocated Bac Stop   
5  damages.6
